subsections.subsection_title: 1. What the OSCE station may say

items.text: You are asked to perform a vulval examination on a woman presenting with vulval itching.
Examine a patient with a painful vulval lump and report your findings.
A woman presents with vulval ulcers. Describe the examination and give your differential diagnoses.
A 60-year-old woman presents with persistent vulval irritation. Examine her and outline further investigations.
Examine a patient with a suspected Bartholin gland cyst.
A photograph shows a white plaque on the vulva. Describe the lesion and discuss the likely diagnosis.
A woman has a pigmented vulval lesion. Explain how you would assess it and identify features concerning for malignancy.

blocks.text: Model introduction

Good morning. My name is Dr. … I understand that you have come for an examination of the external genital area. I would like to examine the skin and surrounding structures to look for any swelling, irritation, ulcers or other abnormalities. This is an intimate examination, so I will explain each step, ensure your privacy and offer a chaperone. You can ask me to pause or stop at any time. Do you have any pain at the moment, and are you happy for me to proceed?

items.text: Wash your hands and use appropriate personal protective equipment.
Confirm the patient's identity and explain the indication for examination.
Obtain informed consent.
Offer a trained chaperone and document the offer and outcome according to local policy.
Ask about pain, allergies to examination materials and relevant previous experiences.
Ensure adequate lighting, a warm examination room and privacy.
Expose only the area necessary for the examination.
Position the patient comfortably, usually in the dorsal lithotomy position, with the knees flexed and hips abducted.
Explain that you will inspect first and touch the area only as necessary.

blocks.text: OSCE tip: A chaperone is not a substitute for consent. The patient may decline the examination, and you should stop if consent is withdrawn.
Know the following structures and be able to identify them on a diagram:

rows: Fatty prominence over the pubic symphysis
Outer skin folds; may show skin disorders or lesions
Important landmarks when assessing lesions or adhesions
Opening of the urethra, anterior to the vaginal opening
Normal anatomical variation around the introitus
Usually at approximately the 4 and 8 o'clock positions of the vaginal opening
Area between the vaginal opening and anus
May show dermatoses, lesions or evidence of disease extending beyond the vulva

blocks.text: Normal vulval anatomy varies considerably between individuals. Differences in pigmentation, labial size, symmetry, hymenal appearance and pubic hair distribution are not, by themselves, evidence of disease.
With the patient appropriately positioned and the area exposed, inspect the vulva systematically before touching the tissues.

items.text: Mons pubis and distribution of pubic hair.
Labia majora and labia minora.
Clitoris and clitoral hood.
Urethral meatus.
Vaginal introitus and visible hymenal remnants.
Bartholin gland regions.
Perineum and perianal area.

blocks.text: Assess the following features:

rows: Erythema, pallor, white plaques, pigmentation or bruising
Ulcers, vesicles, fissures, excoriations, warts or irregular lesions
Localised or diffuse; unilateral or bilateral
Previous surgery, obstetric trauma or inflammatory disease
Loss of normal labial contours, fusion or clitoral hood adhesions
Breakdown, bleeding, crusting or secondary infection

blocks.text: Do not assume that a normal anatomical variation is pathological. Record what you see rather than making unsupported conclusions.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2: Inspect the labia majora and labia minora

blocks.text: Gently separate the labia only as necessary to visualise the underlying structures.

items.text: Redness and swelling.
Excoriations from scratching.
White, thickened or atrophic skin.
Pigmented lesions.
Genital warts.
Ulcers, fissures or blisters.
Adhesions or loss of normal anatomical landmarks.

blocks.text: If a lesion is present, document its exact location, size, colour, shape, border, surface, number and whether it bleeds or is tender.

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Inspect the clitoris and clitoral hood

items.text: Ulcers or other lesions.
Swelling or tenderness.
Adhesions or difficulty retracting the clitoral hood, where appropriate.
Loss of normal anatomy in chronic vulval dermatoses.

blocks.text: Do not forcibly retract the clitoral hood or manipulate painful or adherent tissues.

content_groups.group_title: Step 4: Inspect the urethral meatus and vaginal introitus

items.text: Urethral caruncle or prolapse.
Redness or visible inflammation.
Discharge.
Ulceration or masses.
Atrophic changes, especially after menopause.
Prolapse or distortion of the introitus.

blocks.text: If the patient reports urinary symptoms, ask about dysuria, urgency, frequency and haematuria. A focused vulval examination alone does not exclude urinary tract pathology.

content_groups.group_title: Step 5: Assess the Bartholin gland regions

blocks.text: The Bartholin glands lie posterolaterally to the vaginal opening, with duct openings classically located near the 4 and 8 o'clock positions.
Inspect for unilateral swelling and, if appropriate and consented, palpate gently.

items.text: Bartholin cyst: often a unilateral, fluctuant or soft swelling that may be painless.
Bartholin abscess: typically painful, tender, swollen and sometimes associated with erythema or fever.
Suspicious mass: a firm, irregular, fixed or persistent mass warrants further assessment.

blocks.text: In a woman aged 40 years or older, or in a postmenopausal woman, a new Bartholin-region mass requires particular attention and usually specialist assessment with consideration of biopsy to exclude malignancy.
Never attempt to squeeze or drain a suspected abscess as part of a routine diagnostic examination.

content_groups.group_title: Step 6: Inspect the perineum and perianal region

items.text: Obstetric scars or tears.
Fissures and excoriations.
Skin lesions extending from the vulva.
Perineal defects or distorted anatomy.
Fistulous openings, where suspected.
Perianal dermatoses or lesions.

blocks.text: Palpation is guided by the presenting complaint. It is not necessary to palpate every normal structure.

blocks.title: If a lump is present, assess gently for:

items.text: Site and dimensions.
Consistency: soft, firm or hard.
Tenderness.
Fluctuation.
Mobility or fixation.
Surface and borders.
Local warmth.
Whether the swelling involves the skin or deeper tissues.

blocks.text: Stop if the patient experiences significant pain or asks you to stop.

items.text: Explain that the examination is complete.
Help the patient cover themselves and get comfortable.
Ask whether they are experiencing any discomfort.
Thank the patient.
Dispose of equipment safely and wash your hands.
Explain your findings and the next steps in understandable language.
Document the findings and the consent and chaperone details as appropriate.

blocks.text: Remember: A speculum examination, bimanual examination or rectal examination is not automatically required during a vulval examination. Extend the examination only when clinically indicated, consented to and appropriate for the station.
A normal examination may be reported as follows:

“The external genitalia are normally developed, with no obvious asymmetry, swelling, ulceration, vesicles, warts, skin discoloration or abnormal pigmentation. The labia majora and minora appear normal, with no visible inflammation or excoriation. The clitoris, urethral meatus and vaginal introitus are unremarkable. There is no visible Bartholin-region swelling, and the perineum and perianal skin appear normal. The examination is otherwise unremarkable.”
Only report structures that you have actually examined. If a structure was not adequately visualised, state that rather than describing it as normal.
This is one of the highest-yield sections for image-based OSCE questions.
A. Vulval erythema and excoriation
Findings: redness, scratch marks, swelling or superficial fissures.

items.text: Vulvovaginal candidiasis.
Contact or irritant dermatitis.
Eczema or lichen simplex chronicus.
Other inflammatory dermatoses.

blocks.text: Ask about itching, discharge, new soaps, pads, detergents and previous treatments.
B. White plaques and vulval architectural changes
Findings: pale, thin or wrinkled skin, fissures, bruising, scarring or fusion of structures.
Possible diagnosis: vulval lichen sclerosus.

Typical symptoms include intense itching, soreness and painful intercourse. Severe or chronic disease may cause architectural changes. Persistent ulcers, thickened areas or suspicious lesions require specialist review and possible biopsy.
C. Vesicles or painful ulcers
Findings: grouped blisters, shallow ulcers, tenderness or crusting.
Possible diagnosis: genital herpes.

Other causes include syphilis, trauma, aphthous ulcers and inflammatory disorders. Clinical appearance alone may not reliably distinguish them; lesion NAAT for herpes and appropriate syphilis testing may be required.
D. Papillary or cauliflower-like lesions
Findings: multiple skin-coloured or pink papillary growths.
Possible diagnosis: anogenital warts, commonly associated with certain HPV types.

Differential diagnoses include benign skin tags and other vulval lesions. Biopsy may be necessary if the appearance is atypical, the lesion is pigmented, indurated, ulcerated or fixed, or the diagnosis is uncertain.
E. Unilateral vulval swelling
Findings: a localised mass near the posterolateral vaginal opening.

items.text: Bartholin duct cyst.
Bartholin abscess.
Epidermal inclusion cyst.
Other benign vulval masses.
Vulval or Bartholin gland malignancy.

blocks.text: Pain, fever, rapid enlargement, fixation, irregularity and age at presentation influence the urgency and investigation plan.
F. Suspicious vulval lesion
Findings may include an irregular ulcer, persistent plaque, nodular mass, abnormal pigmentation, induration or a lesion that bleeds on contact.
Possible diagnosis: vulval cancer or a precancerous lesion.
Other benign and inflammatory conditions can resemble malignancy. Persistent or suspicious lesions require prompt specialist assessment and biopsy where indicated.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to describe a vulval lesion in an OSCE

blocks.text: When shown a photograph, do not jump straight to the diagnosis. Describe the lesion first.
Use this structure:
SITE → SIZE → NUMBER → SHAPE → COLOUR → SURFACE → BORDER → TENDERNESS → ASSOCIATED FINDINGS
For example:

“There is a solitary lesion on the left labium majus, measuring approximately 2 cm in diameter. It is irregularly shaped, erythematous and ulcerated, with an irregular raised border. The lesion appears indurated, and there is no active bleeding visible. These findings are concerning for a suspicious vulval lesion, including possible malignancy. I would arrange urgent specialist assessment and biopsy as indicated.”
If you cannot assess tenderness, induration or mobility from a photograph, do not claim that those features are present.

content_groups.group_title: More examples of abnormal findings and reports

blocks.text: Example 1 — Bartholin cyst

“There is a unilateral, approximately 3 cm, smooth swelling in the left posterolateral aspect of the vaginal opening. It appears well circumscribed, with no obvious surrounding erythema or ulceration. The main differential is a Bartholin duct cyst. I would assess tenderness and consistency with consent, check for features of infection, and plan management according to symptoms and examination findings.”
Example 2 — Bartholin abscess

“There is a unilateral swelling in the left Bartholin gland region with marked tenderness, surrounding erythema and local oedema. The findings suggest a Bartholin abscess. I would assess the patient's temperature and general condition, provide analgesia, and arrange appropriate gynaecological treatment, including drainage when indicated.”
Example 3 — Lichen sclerosus

“There are pale, thin, atrophic plaques affecting the vulval skin, with areas of fissuring and architectural distortion. The appearance is suggestive of vulval lichen sclerosus. I would ask about chronic itching and pain, examine the extent of involvement, and arrange appropriate treatment and follow-up, with biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain or suspicious areas are present.”
Example 4 — Genital herpes

“There are multiple grouped superficial ulcers on an erythematous base affecting the vulval skin. The patient reports pain and burning. The findings are compatible with genital herpes, although other ulcerative conditions must be considered. I would obtain lesion NAAT where available, offer appropriate STI testing and initiate antiviral treatment when clinically indicated.”
Example 5 — Suspected vulval malignancy

“There is an irregular, ulcerated lesion on the vulva with an abnormal surface and suspicious borders. Vulval malignancy is an important differential diagnosis. I would document the lesion's exact site and dimensions, assess relevant inguinal lymph nodes, and arrange urgent specialist referral for assessment and biopsy.”

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Differential diagnoses according to the presenting complaint

rows: Candidiasis, contact dermatitis, lichen sclerosus, lichen simplex chronicus, eczema
Herpes, syphilis, aphthous ulcer, trauma, inflammatory disease, malignancy
Primary syphilis, other ulcerative conditions, malignancy
Bartholin cyst or abscess, epidermal cyst, other benign or malignant mass
Lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, dermatitis, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia
Benign melanocytic lesion, post-inflammatory pigmentation, vulval melanoma
Anogenital warts, skin tags, benign papillary lesions, neoplasia
Dermatitis, candidiasis, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, vulvodynia

blocks.text: Exam principle: Morphology narrows the differential; history, examination, testing and sometimes biopsy establish the diagnosis.
Investigations depend on the lesion and symptoms. A normal vulval examination does not require routine testing.

rows: Suspicious, persistent, atypical or diagnostically uncertain lesions
Genital ulceration or relevant exposure risk
Suspected cervicitis or relevant sexual exposure
Discharge, itching or suspected vaginal infection
Suspicious vulval lesion or suspected malignancy
Specialist documentation and follow-up, with informed consent and secure handling

items.text: Vulval cancer is suspected.
A lesion is persistent or unexplained.
The appearance is atypical or the diagnosis remains uncertain.
There is a suspicious pigmented, thickened, indurated or ulcerated area.
A presumed inflammatory disorder is not responding as expected.
There is concern for vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or another premalignant condition.

blocks.text: Do not repeatedly treat a persistent lesion empirically without reconsidering the diagnosis.
Management should target the underlying cause.

items.text: Identify and stop potential irritants, including perfumed washes and unnecessary topical preparations.
Advise gentle washing and avoidance of scrubbing or douching.
Consider an appropriate emollient or prescribed topical corticosteroid depending on the diagnosis.
Review persistent or atypical lesions and refer when needed.
Treat with an appropriate topical azole or other guideline-recommended antifungal.
In pregnancy, use a topical azole for 7 days and avoid oral fluconazole.
Reassess recurrent or treatment-resistant symptoms rather than assuming every episode is candidiasis.
A potent or ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, commonly clobetasol propionate 0.05%, is standard first-line therapy under an appropriate treatment regimen.
Provide vulval skin-care advice and arrange follow-up.
Monitor for scarring and changes suggestive of malignancy.
Refer when the diagnosis is uncertain, disease is difficult to control, or suspicious lesions develop.
Provide appropriate antiviral treatment, such as aciclovir, according to the episode, timing, pregnancy status and local guideline.
Offer counselling on transmission, recurrences, safer sex and partner communication.
Offer appropriate STI testing.
Arrange urgent specialist input for severe disease, complications or significant concerns in pregnancy.
An asymptomatic cyst may not require intervention.
A symptomatic cyst or abscess may require drainage, often using a Word catheter or another appropriate procedure.
Antibiotics are not routinely necessary for every uncomplicated cyst; use them when there is cellulitis, systemic infection or another clear indication.
A new Bartholin-region mass in a woman aged 40 years or older, particularly after menopause, warrants assessment to exclude malignancy and consideration of biopsy.
Arrange urgent referral to gynaecology or a specialist vulval clinic.
Obtain a biopsy through the appropriate specialist pathway.
Assess inguinal lymph nodes and investigate the extent of disease when indicated.
Avoid destructive treatment of a suspicious lesion before adequate diagnostic assessment.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between the vulva and the vagina?

Answer: The vulva refers to the external female genital structures, including the labia, clitoris, vestibule and vaginal opening. The vagina is the internal muscular canal extending from the vaginal opening to the cervix.
Q2. Where are the Bartholin glands located?
Answer: They lie posterolaterally to the vaginal opening, with their duct openings classically situated at approximately the 4 and 8 o'clock positions.
Q3. How would you differentiate a Bartholin cyst from an abscess?

Answer: A cyst is often a painless, localised swelling. An abscess is usually painful, tender and associated with surrounding inflammation; fever may occur. Clinical assessment is necessary because appearances can overlap.
Q4. What are the characteristic features of lichen sclerosus?

Answer: White, thin or wrinkled plaques, itching, fissuring, bruising and possible scarring or loss of normal vulval architecture. Biopsy is indicated when the diagnosis is uncertain or suspicious changes are present.
Q5. What features of a vulval lesion suggest malignancy?

Answer: Persistent ulceration, induration, irregular borders, a growing mass, abnormal pigmentation, unexplained bleeding, non-healing lesions and suspicious inguinal lymph nodes. These features warrant prompt specialist assessment and biopsy where indicated.
Q6. What is the difference between a primary syphilitic ulcer and genital herpes?

Answer: Primary syphilis classically causes a painless, firm ulcer, whereas genital herpes often causes painful grouped vesicles or superficial ulcers. Neither presentation is universal, so laboratory testing is important.
Q7. When should you examine the inguinal lymph nodes?

Answer: When a suspicious vulval lesion or malignancy is suspected, and when there are significant infections or other findings suggesting lymphadenopathy. Document the size, consistency, tenderness and mobility of any enlarged nodes.
Q8. Does every vulval lump require surgery?

Answer: No. Management depends on the diagnosis and symptoms. An asymptomatic Bartholin cyst may need no intervention, whereas an abscess may require drainage. A suspicious mass requires diagnostic assessment rather than simply being excised or drained without a plan.

items.text: Failing to obtain consent for an intimate examination.
Forgetting to offer a chaperone.
Exposing the patient unnecessarily.
Inspecting the labia but forgetting the clitoris, urethral meatus, Bartholin regions, perineum and perianal skin.
Describing a lesion simply as “abnormal” without documenting its site, size, colour, surface and borders.
Diagnosing genital herpes or syphilis solely from appearance.
Failing to consider biopsy for a persistent or suspicious lesion.
Attempting to drain a Bartholin abscess during a routine examination.
Missing the importance of a new Bartholin-region mass in an older or postmenopausal woman.
Forgetting to explain the findings and proposed next steps to the patient.

blocks.text: Visualise all external genital structures systematically.
Urethral meatus and vaginal introitus: inspect carefully.
Labia and lesions: document location, size, colour and morphology.
Vulval lumps: assess the Bartholin regions and other swellings.
Anal and perineal area: inspect and complete the examination.
**Lesion description — “SITE”**

items.text: S — Site and size.
I — Inspection of colour, shape and surface.
T — Tenderness, texture and tissue involvement.
E — Edges, extent and associated findings.
